en: The Western Aspiration Text:
The Great Structural Divisions are two.
First, the general introduction consisting of the homage and salutation; second, the actual presentation of the aspiration text.
Part One: General Preface on Taking Refuge and Paying Homage (in three sections):
1. Identifying the Principal; 2. Clarifying the Vow; 3. Requesting Empowerment. Part Two:
The Actual Text of the Vow (in three sections).
I. The Primary Cause for Seeking Rebirth in the Western Land; II. Clear Evidence of Attaining Rebirth in the Western Land;
III. The Great Function of Having Already Been Born in the Pure Land.
(Section I: The Primary Cause for Seeking Rebirth in the Western Land—Five)
1. Initially arousing the great mind; 2. Repenting of karmic obstacles; 3.
Establishing vows and self-restraint; 4. Seeking the Buddha’s secret empowerment;
5. Accomplishing the purification of karma.
II. The Clear Evidence of Attaining Rebirth in the Western Land:
A. Right Mindfulness at the Moment of Death; B. The Buddha’s Appearance to Welcome One; C. Rebirth in Sukhāvatī; D.
The Great Function of Having Already Been Born in the Pure Land.

An Explanation of the Vow Text for Universally Dedication toward the Western Pure Land: 1. First, seeing the Buddha and receiving the prediction; 2. Second, being granted the prediction and possessing virtuous qualities; 3.
Third, accomplishing benefit for others and bringing forth the welfare of beings; 4. Fourth, universally dedicating all merits toward the West.
Written and explained by the Disciple of Pure Practice, Zhu Hong.
△ First, the General Preface: Paying Homage in Three Parts. 1. Identifying the Principal; 2. Clarifying the Vow; 3. Requesting the Bestowal of Blessings. 1. Identifying the Principal.
I bow my head to the Great Teacher who receives and guides sentient beings in the Western Land of Peace and Bliss.
"Bowing my head" means to strike one's head against the ground, expressing the utmost reverence.

Regarding the phrase "the Western land," it refers to the Land of Peace and Bliss in the west to whom I now offer my devotion; "Peace and Bliss" (Anle) is a synonym for "Ultimate Bliss" (Jile). It is also known as...
"An-yang" (Peaceful Nurturing) is also called "Qing-tai" (Pure Tranquility); their meanings are one and the same. "Jie" (receiving) means to take up; "qi" (guiding) means to lead.
Sentient beings are submerged and sinking; they are received and placed upon the ground of goodness. Sentient beings are deluded and obscured; they are guided back to the correct path.
All spiritual teachers—whether *śrāvakas*, *arhats*, *bodhisattvas*, or *tathāgatas*—are guides who receive and lead, just as there are hunters in a hunt.
The forest officer crosses the river because there is a boat; the elder asks for the way because there are people of the land.
Only the Buddha is the Great Guide among all guides. This "Great" has two meanings: first, because he universally delivers all spirits without exception;
second, because he attains ultimate Buddhahood without regression. △ Second, clarifying his vows.
I now make this vow: may I be reborn in the three pure lands of faith, practice, and vows.
Regarding these provisions for the pure lands, when one speaks only of "vows," it is because there is only faith that leads to the vow.

That which is most earnest in its vow is precisely where its faith is true. Practice is established by means of the vow; that which is most earnest in its vow will naturally be able to put it into practice.
This is why the *Amitābha Sūtra* exclusively emphasizes making vows, with the aspiration to be reborn there being more than sufficient.
△ Third, the request for empowerment:
"I pray that you, out of your compassion, will graciously accept me."
The Vow-text is complete. Someone may ask: "The ancients said, 'One cannot lead another by the hand; only when a person themselves is willing can there be resonance.
Why, then, do you seek the Buddha's reception? Answer: First, it is because of the power of Amitābha’s Original Vow;
second, seeking the Buddha’s reception is itself the act of being willing; third, the mutual resonance of cause and response is precisely what constitutes true resonance.

Therefore (the preceding thirty-six characters are incomplete; now continued). △ Second, the actual exposition of the vow-text, divided into three parts: First, the primary cause for seeking rebirth in the Western Land;
Second, clear evidence of having attained rebirth in the Western Land; Third, the great function once born in the Pure Land.

First, the primary cause for seeking rebirth in the Western Land, divided into five sections: First, generating the Great Mind; Second, repenting and eliminating karmic obstacles; Third, establishing the vow.
First, regarding the initial arousal of the great mind:

(Disciple [Name] and the assembly), universally for the sake of the four debts of gratitude, the three realms of existence, and all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm, seek the unsurpassed Bodhi-path of the One Vehicle of all Buddhas;
therefore, with single-minded devotion, we hold in mind the vast and majestic name of Amitābha Buddha, aspiring to be born there.

"Pure Land" refers first to the fundamental aspiration of reciting the Buddha's name to seek rebirth in the Pure Land. "Universally for all" means harboring the intention to benefit others as well, rather than seeking liberation for oneself alone.
"One Vehicle" means taking the fruit of Buddhahood as one's goal, rather than [stopping at] other [lesser vehicles].
To harbor expectations based on delusion and to give rise to such a mind while practicing the Pure Land is what is called the "correct cause.

If it were otherwise, even if one were diligent in reciting the Buddha’s name, the causal ground would not be true, and the resulting fruit would be circuitous. Regarding the four debts of gratitude (*catvāri ṛṇāni*):
for the laity, these are parents, sentient beings, the sovereign, and the Triple Gem; for those who have left the home life, they are parents, teachers, the sovereign, and [the Sangha].
The King is the donor. The "three realms of existence" (*tridhātu*) consist of the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and the realm of formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*).

△ Second, the repentance for eliminating karmic obstructions: Furthermore, because karma is heavy and merit is light, obstructions are deep and wisdom is shallow; thus, defiled minds easily flare up while pure virtues are difficult to accomplish. Now, at this time...
Before the Buddha, with uplifted diligence, I prostrate my five limbs and lay them bare; with single-minded sincerity, I repent for myself and all sentient beings:
from boundless kalpas until now, we have been deluded regarding our inherently pure mind, allowing greed, anger, and ignorance to defile the three karmas.
May all the immeasurable and boundless stains of sin committed, and the immeasurable and boundless karmic retributions of enmity incurred, be entirely extinguished.

Building upon the above, although one has resolved upon the Great Mind (*mahācitta*), there is fear that due to many karmic obstructions from past lives and the present life, as well as a lack of merit and wisdom, one’s partial defilements may remain uncleansed;
therefore, it is necessary to perform repentance. That which is fundamentally pure means that the mind is inherently pure by nature, yet through delusion it became defiled;

now, for the first time, one awakens to this realization and practices with shame, remorse, and self-reflection. If the mind were not fundamentally pure, it would be like attempting to forge true gold from raw, stubborn iron.
Even if subjected to a hundred refinements, it will ultimately not achieve success. Regarding the three types of karma: they are bodily karma, mental karma, and verbal karma.
Each of these three karmas is possessed of greed, hatred, and delusion. △ Third, the formalization of vows and self-restraint.
From this day forth, I establish profound vows: to remain far removed from unwholesome dharmas and vow never to create them again;
to diligently cultivate the Noble Path and vow never to fall back or become indolent; to attain perfect enlightenment and vow to deliver all sentient beings.
Although one has already performed repentance, if one does not give rise to a vow, this is called "having repentance but no vow.

This "vow" (yào) is like what is commonly called "coercion" today or "pressuring the sovereign" in ancient times; here, it refers to making a commitment for oneself. Thus, the four phrases are the Four Great Vows. The phrase "far removed" corresponds to the vow:
"I vow to sever all afflictions, which are inexhaustible. The phrase "diligently cultivate" corresponds to the vow: "The Dharma gates are immeasurable..."
The phrase "vow to learn" refers to the vow to attain the unsurpassed Buddha-way;
the phrase "vow to accomplish" refers to the vow to save boundless sentient beings. △ Fourth, seeking the Buddha’s secret empowerment.
May Amitābha Buddha, by the power of his compassionate vows, bear witness to me, have pity on me, and bestow his grace upon me. May I,
within my meditative contemplation and even during my dreams, behold the golden body of Amitābha Buddha,
traverse the jewel-adorned land of Amitābha Buddha, and receive the nectar empowerment from Amitābha Buddha.
The light shines upon his body; he strokes my head with his hand and covers my body with his robe.

The *Ancient Text on the Pure Land* states that because the Buddha perceives from afar with his divine eye, hears from afar with his divine ear, and swiftly beholds the minds of others, once the practitioner has resolved upon the Great Mind, the Buddha will certainly bear witness to it. Having thus witnessed it, the Buddha’s great compassion [arises].
May you surely grant your compassionate pity; having granted your pity, the Buddha, with his great majestic power, will surely bestow his grace.
Whether manifest as in meditative contemplation or subtle as in a dream, that which is spoken of—the golden, jewel-adorned hand of radiant nectar-light—will touch and cover one’s robes.
When sincerity reaches its ultimate limit, the response occurs spontaneously; if one is not sincere, or if sincerity has not reached its ultimate limit, then it will not.
It is possible; however, the practitioner need only maintain single-minded sincerity and need not, on this account, give rise to a deliberate effort to seek immediate manifestation.
△ Fifth, the accomplishment of pure karma:
"May my past obstacles be naturally eliminated, my roots of goodness increase, afflictions be swiftly emptied, and ignorance suddenly shattered, so that perfect enlightenment is realized."
The wondrous mind is vast and open, awakening to the true realm of *sambhogakāya* (Jikō), which is constantly manifest before one.
Having attained this through both one’s own power and the grace of the Buddha—this internal and external mutual support—hindrances are extinguished and goodness arises.
Such are the great benefits; though it is empty, it is called "swift," for there is no need for strenuous effort in cultivation or realization. Thus it is broken... [text ends].

It is said that "sudden" means not passing through stages or gradations. Upon realizing that *yuanjue* (perfect enlightenment) is eternally abiding in the realm of quiescent light (*jiguang*), one attains the originally pure mind;
therefore, it is said that "pure karma is accomplished. Regarding "past obstructions," these refer to greed, anger, and delusion;

regarding "roots of goodness," these refer to precepts, concentration, and wisdom. When speaking in terms of the wondrous mind and the true realm, they appear to be distinct, yet in reality, they are identical with the mind itself.
The object is precisely the object; the object is precisely the mind—two yet non-dual. △ Second, the clear evidence of attaining birth in the Western Land, in three parts:
first, maintaining right mindfulness at the time of death; second, the Buddha’s coming to welcome one; third, rebirth in Sukhāvatī. First, maintaining right mindfulness at the time of death.

When approaching the end of life, they know in advance that the time has come; their bodies are free from all illness, suffering, and calamities, and their minds are free from all attachment and delusion.
Their faculties are joyful and serene, their right mindfulness is clear and distinct, and they relinquish the retribution of birth with composure, as if entering a state of meditative concentration.
As for those who have previously cultivated pure causes, they experience this pure retribution at the moment of death.

Those whose daily minds are distracted by miscellaneous thoughts may feel wavering, agitated, and terrified as they approach their end; yet if they can reach a state of single-mindedness, how could their final moments not be settled?
Practitioners need only value being free from attachment and delusion; they need not worry about encountering the suffering of illness.
Should you encounter the calamity of illness, you must know that for one who recites the Buddha’s name, death leads to rebirth in the Pure Land.
Is this not as joyful as casting off tattered rags to don precious robes, or as emerging from a prison to return to one’s ancestral home?

Furthermore, since the ancients asked, "Is there anyone who does not fall ill? it follows that there are likewise those who do not encounter such calamities; what cause for anxiety is there? [Section on Sickness and Suffering]
Those who encounter calamities arising from their own bodies, or those who are possessed by greed—whether for their kin or for their wealth—and are unable to renounce them;
those who are deluded, whose thoughts are inverted, such as not knowing of hell yet saying, "I wish to go there," "I wish to go there. △ Second, the Buddha’s coming to welcome them.
Amitābha Buddha, together with the assembly of holy sages Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, emit light to welcome and guide, extending their hands to support and lead.
With celestial palaces, banners, pennants, extraordinary fragrances, and divine music, the sacred realm of the West is revealed before one's eyes,
causing all sentient beings who see or hear it to rejoice, feel moved, and resolve to attain Bodhicitta.

The Sūtra states: "When one who holds the Name with single-mindedness and without confusion approaches the end of life, Amitābha Buddha, together with the assembly of holy ones, will appear before them.
This is precisely what is meant. If the multitude witness [the manifestation] and thereby arouse the aspiration for enlightenment, then both self and others benefit.
Furthermore, if all people see this event, it is truly a sign of personal realization; however, if only the individual sees it while others do not, it may be a demonic affair.
△ Third, Rebirth in Sukhāvatī: At that time,
I shall mount a vajra-throne and follow behind the Buddha, and in the time it takes to snap one's fingers,
I shall be born within a sublime lotus flower in a pool of the seven treasures in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Seeing the Buddha coming above, one now follows the Buddha in departing; this coming and departing occurs within the state of no-coming-and-no-going. That which surpasses the lotus is the "superior-superior" grade.

△ Third, the Great Function of those already born in the Pure Land, in four parts: First, seeing the Buddha and receiving a prediction; Second, being endowed with virtues upon receiving the prediction;
Third, accomplishing benefit for sentient beings; Fourth, universally dedicating all merit. First, seeing the Buddha and receiving [the prediction]:
Record:
Upon the blossoming of the flower, he beheld the Buddha and the various bodhisattvas; hearing the sublime sound of the Dharma, he attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
In an instant, he served all the Buddhas and personally received their prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).

The previous statement spoke of seeking birth in the Pure Land during one's lifetime and attaining such birth at the moment of death; however, how could it be that merely attaining birth is sufficient?

Now, it is said that after attaining birth, one personally receives a prediction of enlightenment from the Buddha, becomes fully endowed with merit, and extensively delivers sentient beings—such are the great functions [of this attainment].
For all who are born in the Western Land, there are differences in the speed with which their lotuses bloom and the timing of when they behold the Buddha.

The realization of the Way attained later has its earlier and later stages; now, at the very moment of raising a thought, there is birth, and as soon as one is born, flowers bloom, one sees the Buddha, hears the Dharma, attains patience (*kṣānti*), and receives a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). These are all matters of the highest grade.
△ Second, receiving the prediction and possessing merit.

Having received the prophecy, one fully accomplishes all merits—the three bodies, the four wisdoms, the five eyes, the six supernormal powers, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *dhāraṇī* gates.
One might wonder: "How can such vast merits, which require cultivation over many eons, be attained in a single [lifetime]?"
Those born in the Western Land all achieve complete fulfillment; not knowing that the myriad dharmas are but mind, once they have attained this single mind, what dharma could they not attain?
Mañjuśrī’s *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra calls mindfulness of the Buddha the "Single Practice Samādhi" (*ekavyūha-samādhi*).
Having attained this samādhi, one's extensive learning, wisdom, and eloquence far exceed those of Ānanda by hundreds of thousands of millions of times—the rest may be known by inference.

...Thus it is. The three bodies are the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body. The four wisdoms are the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, the Equality Wisdom, the Wondrous Observing Wisdom, and the Accomplishing-What-is-to-be-Done Wisdom.
The five eyes are the flesh eye, the heavenly eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye, and the Buddha eye.

The six supernormal powers are the power of the heavenly eye, the heavenly ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, the power of spiritual mobility, and the power of the exhaustion of outflows.
Furthermore, "dhāraṇī" is translated here as "total retention" (zǒngchí).

△ Third, having accomplished benefits for others and brought beings to maturity, he then does not remain in peace in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, but returns to the Sahā world, manifesting countless emanations throughout the lands of the ten directions.
By means of inconceivable and sovereign spiritual powers and various skillful means, he delivers and liberates sentient beings, causing them all to leave defilement behind and return [to the source].
May those who attain a pure mind be reborn together in the Western Land and enter the stage of non-retrogression;
as long as this great vow, the world, sentient beings, karma, and afflictions are all inexhaustible, may my vow remain inexhaustible.

Those of the latter category are what the ancients called those who, having already attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) in the Western Land, return to this world to save suffering sentient beings.
Those who enter without contradiction constantly dwell within the nine grades and are ever present throughout the ten directions;
from moment to moment they are capable of enduring to deliver sentient beings, and at every instant they enter right concentration (*samādhi*) in the West, thereby regaining a pure mind.

The previous statement spoke of being deluded regarding the fundamentally pure mind; this statement speaks of having been deluded in the past and now attaining awakening. It is like having long lost one’s direction and finally finding it:
one recovers the originally existing pure mind rather than newly acquiring it.

"Wishing for them to be inexhaustible" means that because they previously gave rise to the unsurpassed great resolve (*mahācitta*), they have now brought their inexhaustible great vows to fulfillment. △ Fourth, Universal Dedication.

I now pay homage to the Buddha and make this vow to cultivate and maintain merit, dedicating it to all sentient beings so that the four debts of gratitude may be universally repaid, the three realms of existence may be equally sustained,
and all beings throughout the Dharma-realm may together perfect the wisdom of the awakened one.
The initial aspiration to seek birth in the Pure Land was originally for the sake of all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm of the four debts of gratitude and the three realms of existence;
thus, this dedication of merit is likewise.
*Commentary on the Western Vow Text* (End).
Postscript to the Original Edition of the *Western Vow Text* (Xifang yuanwen):
Since the autumn of the year Gui-mao, I have had the honor of attending upon the Master’s compassionate countenance as he expounded this vow text, which has cleared away the clouds of my delusion.
I once inquired why the *Vajra* [Sūtra] encompasses everything; the Master replied: "To speak of non-existence is to have nothing that is not non-existent; to speak of existence..."
"There is nothing that does not exist. Upon hearing these words, he suddenly attained realization. He further inquired about the meaning of "one should give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere.
The Master said, "This can be read as a single phrase, or it can be read as two phrases; both interpretations are consistent with the meaning."
Furthermore, for my sake, you drew upon various analogies to illuminate the complete purport of the *Prajñāpāramitā* in its entirety; I truly began to understand its direction.

I am deeply grateful that you, my teacher, were like Amitāyus, yet you have suddenly entered parinirvāṇa. My grief and lamentation are beyond measure. Though your golden countenance is now obscured, your golden mouth ever proclaims the Dharma.
I have carved this vow-text to commemorate the beginning of my refuge, wishing that it may endure as long as the future reaches its end.
As for those students of the future who see, hear, and rejoice in this, may they, in every thought-moment, awaken to Amitāyus and, with single-mindedness and without distraction,
all enter the great ocean of vows of Yunqi.
Eulogy for the Portrait of the Great Master Yunqi:

The marrow of Chan, the thoroughfare of Confucianism, the tiger of the Vinaya, and the dragon of the Teaching. With the *ekavyūha-samādhi* as his core practice, he took the methods of subduing and gathering as his fundamental principle.
Adorning the myriad virtues, the provisional and the real are unified. But tell me, where is this unification perceived? Heh!
The moon beneath the water is the moon in the sky; the wind in the valley is the wind atop the ridge.
In the past, when the descendant of Duke Mu [Zigong] spoke of the Bodhisattva Rujung, he praised my words daily as if using both hands to carry soil added to Mount Tai;
yet when speaking of the Great Master, he was like one picking up a mote of dust with a single finger.
It is wafted upon the peak of Mount Sumeru, merely to express the faint traces of my yearning and admiration.
Written by the disciple Guangdan on the first day of the winter month in the forty-third year of the Wanli era, with humble greetings.
